newsitem.title: USA: UAW, GM reach tentative pact to end plant strike.
newsitem.headline: UAW, GM reach tentative pact to end plant strike.

text.p: The United Auto Workers said they reached a tentative agreement with General Motors Corp. on Friday night, ending a three-day strike that might have crippled GM's North American production within a week.

Details of the agreement, reached about 9:30 p.m. EDT (0031 GMT on Saturday), were being withheld until members of UAW Local 909 in Warren, Michigan, held a ratification vote on Sunday, Jim Marcum, financial secretary of the union, said.
"It's a done deal," Marcum said, adding that bargaining team members were pleased with the results.
"They just said they were very happy, and we'll be very happy," he said.
About 2,800 members of Local 909 walked off the job at midnight on Tuesday when a new three-year contract had not been reached by a strike deadline.
The plant supplies automatic transmissions for many of GM's front-wheel-drive cars and wheels and suspension control arms for both cars and light trucks.
A shortage of parts forced GM to start shutting down plants within a day of the strike. As of Friday, it had idled four car plants in Michigan and two at its Oshawa, Ontario, complex.

The shutdowns affected about 16,500 workers, not including the strikers, and led to fears that production disruptions would quickly spread to the rest of GM's North American assembly facilities by the end of next week.
As they have with previous settlements, GM officials said the agreement allowed the company to be competitive and also satisfied its employees.
"We believe the agreement addresses the legitimate needs of our employees, while at the same time it enables GM to meet our needs to be more competitive," GM spokeswoman Darla Park said.

Two strikes in the second quarter, one at GM's Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, plant for Malibu and Cutlass cars and another at its Pontiac, Michigan, plant for full-size pickup trucks, cost the carmaker $490 million in lost profits.

So far this year, GM has been hit with six strikes. The No. 1 U.S. carmaker has resisted union demands to add jobs as it tries to reduce its workforce through attrition and to pare manufacturing costs.

In Warren the union had demanded that GM add several hundred workers to the plant to offset retirements and ease overtime strains. The union also wanted GM to put a cap on products it planned to obtain from outside suppliers.

GM had reportedly offered to transfer torque converter work to the plant to substitute for wheel work it wanted to move to an outside supplier. But that would have meant loss of the torque converter production by UAW workers at GM's Buick City complex in Flint, Michigan. Torque converters are used in auto transmissions.

Workers at a Delphi Interior & Lighting Systems plant in Anderson, Indiana, are scheduled to ratify a new agreement on Saturday. Not including the Warren and Anderson workers, nine of GM's 105 UAW locals still do not have new three-year agreements.
